content_voiceover: This slide covers the protein C anticoagulation pathway, the body's main brake on thrombin generation, and it contrasts two functional states of the very same complex. On the left, you have prothrombinase, built from factor ten a, factor five a, an anionic phospholipid membrane, and calcium, this complex takes factor two, prothrombin, and converts it into thrombin, factor two a, that's the normal procoagulant function we've been discussing. But thrombin has a second job once it diffuses to intact endothelium. On the right side, thrombin binds thrombomodulin on the endothelial surface, and that thrombin, thrombomodulin, anionic membrane, calcium complex is now called protein C ase, because its substrate has switched entirely, instead of clotting factors, it activates protein C into activated protein C, or APC. Notice the red circle with the slash on the left, once thrombin is bound to thrombomodulin, it can no longer cleave fibrinogen, that's a critical concept, thrombomodulin binding redirects thrombin's specificity away from procoagulant substrates and toward protein C. Once APC is generated, it moves to the phospholipid surface shown on the lower right, and together with its cofactor protein S, it proteolytically inactivates factor eight a and factor five a, the two cofactors that are essential for the tenase and prothrombinase complexes. By destroying eight a and five a, APC shuts down thrombin generation and terminates the coagulation cascade. This pathway is why protein C or protein S deficiency causes a hypercoagulable state, and it's also the mechanism behind factor five Leiden, a mutation that makes factor five a resistant to APC cleavage, which is the single most common inherited thrombophilia.
keypoints: Prothrombinase (Xa, Va, membrane, calcium) converts prothrombin to thrombin
Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin loses its ability to cleave fibrinogen
Thrombin-thrombomodulin complex instead activates protein C to APC
APC with cofactor protein S degrades factors VIIIa and Va
This pathway explains hypercoagulability in protein C/S deficiency and factor V Leiden
keypoint_voiceover: Prothrombinase makes thrombin, but once thrombin binds thrombomodulin on endothelium, it stops clotting fibrinogen and instead activates protein C. Activated protein C, with protein S as cofactor, degrades factors eight a and five a, shutting down thrombin generation. This is why protein C or S deficiency, and factor five Leiden, cause hypercoagulable states.
